strengths: Clear, intuitive analytical explanation: The paper provides a neat and theoretically grounded explanation for why tuning the value bias ($b_v$) is significantly more effective than query ($b_q$) or key ($b_k$) biases—specifically showing how shift-invariance neutralizes $b_k$, the softmax Jacobian dampens $b_q$, whereas $b_v$ passes directly through attention as an unconstrained additive term ($a(V + b_v) = aV + b_v$).

Extensive empirical evaluation: The central claim is validated across an impressive variety of models (BERT, RoBERTa, OPT-1.3B/6.7B, and bias-free models such as LLaMA-2-7B, GPT-J-6B, and DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B) across classification, multiple-choice, and generative QA tasks.

Comprehensive exploration and rigor: The authors include statistical significance tests (paired t-tests), multi-seed runs with standard deviations, and explore combinations of bias tuning with other PEFT formulations (LoRA, VeRA, DoRA).
weaknesses: Practical utility of the selection metric vs. static recommendation: The paper spends considerable effort defining a post-hoc angular-magnitude metric $\Delta(b_T)$ to rank bias importance, yet the paper's ultimate actionable takeaway is that practitioners should simply pick $b_v$ directly without running any post-hoc profiling. The dual framing between introducing a dynamic ranking metric and advocating a static selection heuristic feels slightly disconnected.

Marginal parameter-saving benefits over standard BitFit: While reducing trainable parameters from ~0.1% (all biases) to ~0.01% ($b_v$ only) is technically an order-of-magnitude reduction, the absolute memory footprint of storing all biases in modern LLMs is already negligible. In higher-data regimes, bias-only tuning also trails weight adaptation methods.

Visual artifacts and layout polish: Figure 3 and Figure 6 suffer from visual glitches, including duplicate overlapping legends, draft boxes, and crowded sub-captions (e.g., repeated labels '(a) Magnitude (b) Fisher ...').

strengths: Clear, intuitive analytical justification: The paper provides an elegant explanation for why different attention bias terms behave differently—demonstrating that key bias $b_k$ is absorbed due to softmax shift-invariance, query bias $b_q$ has muted influence due to softmax saturation/sharpness, while value bias $b_v$ acts as a direct, unconstrained additive shift to the output representation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The authors substantiate their claims across encoder-only models (BERT, RoBERTa), decoder-only autoregressive models (OPT up to 6.7B), and bias-free models (LLaMA-2, GPT-J, DeepSeek-Coder) across diverse NLU, multiple-choice, and generation benchmarks.

Remarkable parameter efficiency in low-data regimes: Updating only $b_v$ reduces trainable parameters down to ~0.01%–0.04‰ of the total model size while matching or outperforming full fine-tuning and all-bias fine-tuning in data-constrained scenarios.

Extensive investigation of extensions: The paper thoughtfully explores combining bias tuning with low-rank techniques (LoRA, VeRA, DoRA, PiSSA), verifying the stability across random seeds, and providing rigorous statistical significance testing via paired t-tests.
weaknesses: Duality between selection metric and universal rule: The paper dedicates significant attention to the 'magnitude + angle' change metric $\Delta(b_T)$, which requires an initial round of fine-tuning all biases (post-hoc). However, the paper simultaneously advocates a direct, static heuristic ('just fine-tune $b_v$ without post-hoc evaluation'). Streamlining the presentation to clarify whether the metric is primarily an analytical tool or an operational algorithm would improve focus.

Clarification on $b_k$ behavior during optimization: Because the softmax row-wise operation is strictly shift-invariant to the scalar broadcast $q b_k^T$, in standard multi-head attention the output has zero derivative with respect to $b_k$ (i.e., $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial b_k = 0$). The paper should clarify whether $b_k$ received zero gradients in standard attention layers and whether the observed performance changes for $b_k$ were entirely driven by the task-specific classification head updates.

Scope limited mainly to low-data regimes: The empirical superiority of tuning solely $b_v$ diminishes as training data scales towards full datasets, where higher-capacity adaptation methods (like standard LoRA or full-parameter tuning) naturally surpass single-vector bias tuning. A more detailed discussion on the exact boundary conditions where practitioners should transition from BEFT to matrix-level PEFT would add practical value.

strengths: Clear and actionable empirical takeaway: The paper identifies that fine-tuning only the value bias ($b_v$) in self-attention captures almost all the adaptation capability of bias-only tuning (BitFit) while requiring significantly fewer trainable parameters and runtime.

Sound theoretical intuition: The authors explain why key bias ($b_k$) has minimal impact in standard attention due to the shift-invariance of the softmax operator, and show that value bias ($b_v$) acts as an unconstrained post-attention additive shift equivalent to the output projection bias.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments span encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder-only models (OPT-1.3B, OPT-6.7B), as well as bias-free architectures (LLaMA-2, DeepSeek-Coder, GPT-J), across classification, multiple-choice, and generation benchmarks.
Good rigor regarding reproducibility: The appendix includes standard deviations across seeds, paired t-tests confirming statistical significance, and hyperparameter tables.
weaknesses: Severe visual formatting artifacts in figures: Figure 3 and Figure 6 appear to contain unedited/duplicated draft components, overlaid bounding boxes, and repetitive caption snippets that distract from readability and diminish presentation quality.

Over-engineered importance metric: The derivation of the 'Magnitude + Angle' projection metric in Section 2 feels somewhat ad-hoc and secondary, given that the simple mathematical explanation (softmax shift invariance for $b_k$ and linear additive bypass for $b_v$) already explains the phenomena much more cleanly.

Neglect of modern positional embeddings (e.g., RoPE): The theoretical derivation that $b_k$ cancels out holds strictly for absolute positional embeddings where $b_k$ is identical across all key positions. When rotary embeddings (RoPE) are applied to keys, $R_{	heta, j} b_k$ varies by position and no longer cancels out. The paper should explicitly analyze or clarify this interaction, especially when evaluating LLaMA-2.

Limited scope of novelty: While the finding that $b_v$ is the primary effective bias term is neat and practical, the broader framework of bias-only tuning in low-data regimes is already well established by BitFit and related work.
